---
title: "Quiz: the generalised Hough transform"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. The R-table stores, for each gradient-direction bin, the vectors from the template's edge points to its reference point.

---

**Q1.** What is stored in the R-table, and why is it indexed by the edge direction?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does an edge point in a new image know about itself?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
For each edge point of the template, the vector from the point to the reference point, filed under the point's gradient direction. In a new image an edge point knows only its position and its direction; the direction narrows down where on the shape it can be, and so which vectors can lead to the reference point.
:::

---

**Q2.** A direction bin of the R-table holds 20 vectors. An edge point of the scene falls into that bin. How many votes does it cast, and how many of them can be correct?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The point lies at one place on the shape.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
20 votes, one per vector. If the point belongs to a copy of the shape, at most one of them (the vector of its own position on the boundary, or a few if several template points are very close) lands on the reference point; the others land elsewhere. Only the correct votes of many points pile up; the wrong ones spread out.
:::

---

**Q3.** Why is the circle Hough transform with gradient voting and a known radius a special case of the generalised Hough transform?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Build the R-table of a disc with its centre as the reference point.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
On a disc each gradient direction occurs at one point of the boundary, and from there the centre is at distance $r$ along the gradient. So the R-table has one vector per direction, of length $r$ along the direction; voting with it puts one vote at $\mathbf p + r\mathbf u$, which is exactly circle voting with a known radius and polarity.
:::

---

**Q4.** The template is a key; in the scene the key is rotated by 60°. Without a rotation search it is not found. Why not?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Two things change under a rotation.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The gradient directions of the rotated key are all 60° larger, so its edge points look up the wrong bins; and even with the right bin, the stored vectors point in the unrotated directions. Its votes scatter instead of meeting. A rotation search shifts the bin index and rotates the vectors for each tried angle.
:::

---

**Q5.** Searching 36 rotations and 5 scales: how much more work and memory than translation only?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
One accumulator slice per pose.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$36 \times 5 = 180$ poses: 180 lookups per edge point instead of 1, and 180 accumulator slices instead of 1. That is why the search is done coarse to fine: all poses on a small image, then only the best ones at full resolution.
:::

---

**Q6.** A third of a copy is hidden behind another object. Is it still found?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which votes are lost?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Usually yes: the visible two thirds still vote for the same reference point, giving about two thirds of the full peak. It is found if that is above the threshold; the threshold works as a minimum visible fraction of the boundary.
:::

---

**Q7.** Why can a shape that is merely similar to the template (say, a key with a longer shaft) be reported as a detection?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many of its edge points vote correctly?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Large parts of its boundary coincide with the template's after a shift: those points vote for (nearly) the same reference point and produce a peak that may reach a third or more of a full match. With a low threshold it is accepted. A higher threshold, or checking the whole outline afterwards, rejects it.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that with a single direction bin the generalised Hough transform is the correlation of the scene's edge map with the template's edge map.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Write the votes at $\mathbf c$ as a double sum and substitute $\mathbf q = -\mathbf v$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
With one bin, every edge point votes with every vector: $H(\mathbf c) = \sum_{\mathbf x}\sum_{\mathbf v \in T} E(\mathbf x)[\mathbf x + \mathbf v = \mathbf c] = \sum_{\mathbf v \in T} E(\mathbf c - \mathbf v)$. With $\mathbf q = -\mathbf v$, the template edge points relative to the reference point: $H(\mathbf c) = \sum_{\mathbf q} E(\mathbf c + \mathbf q)E_T(\mathbf q)$, the correlation of $E$ with $E_T$. The direction bins restrict each sum to points of the same direction, which makes the match selective.
:::
